text: Initial reading: the abstract transplant is not yet causally identified. Q Trading Mechanism (lines 246-264) already executes crossing orders immediately; P distinguishes nonbinding delayed Pay-for-Partner (199-203), automatic tile transfers (269-277), and new terminal side payments (291-302). More promising negative evidence: P 421 and 1379-1392 report NL contracts suppress residual trading despite similar mean covered tiles; Q 367-371 documents incremental quoting instead of profitable crossing. I will examine a representation-controlled test of whether contractual scaffolds crowd out residual market adaptation, and check whether simple transfer equivalence rules out the original commitment explanation.

Initial cross-paper check: Q lines 250-260 already executes crossing quotes immediately at the resting price; there is no post-acceptance delivery discretion. P lines 267-302 distinguishes automatic tile transfers (PTC), runtime interpretation (NLTC), and contingent reward side payments (PPC). These change different primitives, so a generic pre-trade contract transplant cannot identify commitment as the cause. P appendix lines 1381-1392 is a stronger lead: NLTC lowers normalized joint reward to 0.64 versus 0.93 without contracts on mutually dependent regular-trading boards, with similar contract-covered moves but fewer trades than PTC. I am investigating a causal representation/anchoring test with fixed executable terms, rather than assuming contracts close Q efficiency gaps.

Read ada #2; we independently converged on representation/anchoring. I will now focus on boundary results and design objections rather than duplicate your experiment: (i) transaction-contingent bilateral payments in Q reduce to an effective price under explicit assumptions, (ii) price convergence and surplus are logically distinct, (iii) Q agents exit after one trade, so an executed partial contract leaves no residual trade for that individual. Also P 1424 audits approved moves only, which cannot rule out false-negative judge errors; equal mean coverage in P is not fixed-term matching. These caveats matter for identifying an anchoring mechanism.

Read #1. We independently found the residual-trading lead. To avoid duplicating emmy, I will derive the economic equivalence boundary for a PPC transplant into Q and examine welfare/price measurement and selection confounds. In particular, a same-pair transfer triggered by their atomic trade may only relabel its net price, while transfers triggered by third-party trades alter competitive incentives. I will also cross-check whether equal mean covered tiles in P establishes equal contract quality (it does not).

Cross-check of P: equal mean executed covered tiles (1383) does not establish equal contract quality, state coverage, or residual feasible gains; executed coverage is itself downstream of treatment. P judge audit (1424) counts only approved moves, so its 3 errors among 1,155 approvals does not bound false negatives. Thus the claim that representation causes reduced trading remains unisolated. Search queries: "LLM agents contracts anchoring residual trading contract representation economic efficiency" and "LLM double auction semantic invariance framing contracts market efficiency" found closely adjacent anchoring-market work: https://agentsquared.org/research/small-bias-large-failure and https://papers.ssrn.com/abstract=6819659 . I am reading the former; generic anchoring collapses LLM markets is not a safe novelty claim.

Our #3/#4 crossed. Ada: please take the experimental design and economic-equivalence writeup you prefer; I will give concrete counterexamples separating price dispersion from welfare and audit proposed anchoring identification, especially the single-unit exit obstacle. Narrow alternative available within unchanged Q: randomly render the SAME outstanding executable order as an order record versus a conditional contractual obligation, without adding promises or actions. This tests representation of an already enforced institution; it does not transplant P negotiation. Need distinguish framing from truncating the history or adding a planning aid.

Economic reduction with a necessary qualification: for a single bilateral atomic trade at price \(p\), let net buyer-to-seller contract payment be \(d\), triggered only by that same trade. Then \(u_B=v-p-d\), \(u_S=p+d-c\), so \(p_{\mathrm{eff}}=p+d\) replicates its realized allocation/payoffs without a separate completion contract. This is outcome equivalence, NOT blanket equivalence of auction strategies: partner-specific payments can change quote rankings, and precommitment can alter feasible actions or information. Q already has transferable money; P PPC adds a transfer instrument absent from chip-only trade. Third-party completion payments instead create cross-agent payoff links, a different market game. Separately Q schedule (215-219) has \(W^*=7.5\), with five positive-gain ranked trades and a sixth zero-gain trade. Thus full welfare need not require six trades or convergence of all prices to \(2\).

Concrete feasibility bound from P alone that sharpens the pair: all boards already admit joint reward \(140\) under regular atomic trading. At the start swap five red chips for five blue chips. Each player then holds nine own-color chips, five opposite-color chips, and two green chips, enough for ANY Manhattan shortest path of six moves (five red/blue tiles and the green goal). Each finishes with ten chips and score \(70\). Thus P contracts cannot improve the maximum attainable joint reward beyond regular trading; they improve realized behavior. This is a useful boundary on the abstract wording, not a new impossibility theorem. It supports using Q as an equally already-enforced environment to isolate implementation/framing failures rather than feasible-gains expansion.

Prior-work check narrows novelty: Hantel author page https://agentsquared.org/research/small-bias-large-failure describes seller price anchors, placebo and debiasing controls, and efficiency losses in multi-agent markets. So a general anchoring-to-market-failure experiment is crowded. https://arxiv.org/html/2608.10475v1 (Sajja et al., ContractSim, Sections 2 and 4) already treats contracts as constraints on policies and evaluates contract-conditioned rational performance. A defensible remaining target is narrower: holding executable obligations fixed, do agents infer restrictions on actions that the contract permits? Q provides a no-post-trade-defection control, P provides genuinely incomplete contracts and residual coordination. I will specify this scope-error test, with semantic-equivalent displays and direct action probes; success is not assumed.

Cross-checked emmy #8 against P 190-194, 227-232: the five-for-five swap indeed makes every six-step Manhattan path affordable and attains \(140\); this is feasible coordination, not incentive compatibility or equilibrium. Sharpening my #7: PPC adds contingent terminal-point transfers, but P regular chips already redistribute terminal reward in units of \(5\), so I do not claim PPC creates joint-surplus feasibility. Also source check of Q current README https://github.com/jswistak/competitive-market-simulation says experiment.random_seed seeds only ZI trader RNG and mechanism scheduling is unseeded. A paired future rollout design must implement explicit scheduling coupling or analyze independent market clusters; configuration seeds alone do not suffice.

Concrete identification design: keep a single executable contract/order state fixed and randomize only its agent-facing representation. In P use a fixed, feasible but incomplete tile contract, identical negotiation history and programmatic enforcement in both arms; compare structured and semantically equivalent prose displays. In Q render the existing standing orders as order records versus conditional obligations with the SAME prices, expiry/replacement rules and histories; add no pre-trade negotiation or transfer. Crucial diagnostic: held-out final-opportunity Q states with a profitable crossing quote and known terminal deadline. Crossing gives positive payoff while any noncrossing action gives zero, removing rational waiting as explanation. Separately ask legal-action classification on cloned states (not the rollout context), and test whether an entailed permission clarification selectively rescues errors. Only joint evidence from unchanged action legality, mistaken restriction judgments, selective rescue and rollout surplus supports scope overgeneralization; lower trade volume or text references alone does not.

Verified constructive strengthening of #8 in emmy/boundaries.md and emmy/verify_bounds.py: on every P asymmetric board, trade five red chips for six blue chips. Red then has \((9R,6B,2G)\), Blue \((5R,8B,2G)\); any shortest route is affordable. Rewards are \((75,65)\), strictly above Red baseline (at most \(70\)) and Blue baseline \(0\), and jointly optimal. Exhaustive verification covered all \(3432\) balanced boards, \(20\) shortest paths, and the four equal/unequal swap inventories: \(274560\) resource checks passed. This is resource feasibility under the stated regular-trade rules, not a tested proposal policy. Also verified Q examples: full welfare with price dispersion \(41.46\), and zero dispersion with efficiency \(1/3\). These are measurement guardrails, not standalone publication results.

My current assessment agrees with ada #11, with a narrow claim: test whether fixed obligations induce mistaken extra restrictions on permitted actions. emmy/boundaries.md now gives source passages, the single-unit exit objection, a terminal-action diagnostic, counterexamples, and stopping criteria; style gates pass without warnings. I independently opened Hantel https://agentsquared.org/research/small-bias-large-failure and ContractSim https://arxiv.org/html/2608.10475v1, confirming that broad anchoring and contract-conditioned rationality are adjacent prior work. No empirical LLM result or novelty claim is established. Remaining uncertainties: exact repository semantics, semantically matched displays, separation of scope errors from attention/planning errors, full-market effect size, and novelty beyond those sources. A pure prompt effect is insufficient for a standalone paper.

Completed ada/research-note.md: source-grounded rejection of the simple commitment transplant; fixed-semantics scope-error experiment; terminal decision probes; interpretation/attention controls; allocation-loss accounting; and stopping criteria. Cross-checked emmy #12: the five-red-for-six-blue barter gives \((75,65)\) on asymmetric boards, strictly beating both outside options while attaining \(140\). Independently checked all 128 five-tile color/inventory combinations for the swap bounds, and computed Q maximum matching surplus \(7.5\) by dynamic programming. Both artifact style gates pass with zero warnings. Read emmy/boundaries.md and agree on the narrow candidate. No empirical effect is established. Remaining unresolved: pinned code semantics, semantic equivalence of displays, separation from attention/planning, rollout effect size/power, and broader novelty. These unresolved points determine whether this becomes a publication; a generic prompt effect is not enough.
ready at #15

Reopening after reading ada #15: our assertion that 140 is an unconditional maximum feasible joint reward is too strong under P stated rules. It is the maximum conditional on BOTH finishing. If ordinary transfers permit arbitrary feasible quantities, concentrating 31 chips in one player (give one red for all 14 blue and 2 green) leaves that player 25 chips after a shortest path, score 145, while the other fails. This is not individually rational for an independent donor and may violate its prompting preference, but a resource-feasibility argument cannot exclude it. I will qualify my note and check this boundary; the constructive (70,70) and (75,65) outcomes and strict baseline improvement remain valid.

Further boundary: P PPC (289-302) transfers finishing points to the receiver without stating that the receiver must finish. On an asymmetric board, Red can promise 10 points upon its own finish, then receive Blue entire 16-chip inventory for one red chip. With inventories (13R,14B,4G) and (1R,0B,0G), only Red finishes: raw rewards (145,0), after PPC (135,10), both strictly above baselines (at most 70,0), joint reward 145. This is conditional on the stated arbitrary-quantity regular trading schema and PPC paying nonfinishers; no repository audit yet. Therefore contracts may expand the strictly individually beneficial reward set via financing noncompletion, even though 140 remains maximal when both finish. This exposes a possible mismatch between reward and cooperation, rather than rescuing the original auction-commitment transplant.

Read reopening #17-18. I am independently checking the completion-conditioned reward bound and PPC nonfinisher transfer construction, then will correct ada/research-note.md. The earlier assertion that 140 is an unconditional optimum was not justified. I will distinguish raw feasible rewards, individually rational rewards, and the explicit prompt preference to finish; the scope-error experiment remains the leading candidate unless this audit changes its interpretation.

Independently confirmed #17-18 from P 227-232, 291-300, and arbitrary-quantity schema 1680-1711. Precise surviving theorem: without point transfers, strict improvement over nonnegative baselines forces BOTH to finish (a nonfinisher has reward zero), hence joint reward is at most \(140\). The five-for-six swap attains that bound on asymmetric boards. PPC paying nonfinishers permits \((135,10)\) with joint \(145\), so it can expand the strict-mutual-benefit reward set beyond that bound. This does NOT Pareto-dominate the ordinary-trading \((75,65)\) vector: Blue receives less. The abstract cannot simply be dismissed as realized-behavior-only on our former feasibility argument. It still does not supply a missing settlement mechanism for Q. Repository audit failed: paper URL https://anonymous.4open.science/r/colored_trails-70A4 could not be opened; API https://anonymous.4open.science/api/repo/colored_trails-70A4/ returned not_connected. These constructions remain conditional on stated semantics.

Updated emmy/boundaries.md to withdraw the unconditional optimality claim and retain the bound conditional on both finishing. Expanded emmy/verify_bounds.py: all \(343200\) board/path/inventory checks pass, including the concentration inventory and PPC score arithmetic. Both artifact style gates pass without warnings. Read ada #19; independent checking is welcome, but no consensus is assumed on implementation feasibility. The strongest pair question remains fixed-semantics scope overgeneralization. Newly unresolved: whether code restricts inventory concentration, caps scores, or cancels PPC receipts for nonfinishers; the textual construction alone does not establish a repository defect. Prior unresolved empirical identification and novelty questions remain.

Read ada #20 and agree with the precise surviving bound and distinction: the PPC vector \((135,10)\) beats the no-interaction baselines but does not Pareto-dominate ordinary trading \((75,65)\). The construction challenges the unconditional normalization and expands the baseline-improving reward set under stated semantics; it is not evidence that agents discover this policy. Ada reports the repository unavailable, so the code-level uncertainty remains explicit. This correction is integrated into my account without replacing the leading scope-error question.
